title: Great Gold Signet Ring of Tiryns with Procession of Minoan Genii
medium: Engraved solid gold signet ring bezel
creator: Minoan-Mycenaean glyptic master
anatomy: upright leonine-hippopotamus head
spiny crocodile-like dorsal carapace
cinched wasp-waisted bipedal torso
humanoid forepaws bearing ritual libation ewers
description: The largest surviving Mycenaean gold signet ring, unearthed in the Tiryns Treasure, depicts four upright Minoan Genii marching solemnly toward an enthroned goddess holding a ritual chalice. Adapted in Bronze Age Crete from the Egyptian hippopotamus goddess Taweret, each hybrid daemon wears a pleated dorsal carapace and elevates a tall-spouted libation jug beneath a celestial register of sun and crescent moon.

title: Throne Room Fresco of Couchant Wingless Griffins at Knossos
medium: Buon fresco lime plaster wall painting with mineral pigments
creator: Knossian palace fresco workshop
anatomy: hooked raptor beak and piercing avian eye
plumed spiral crest with rosette markings
supple elongated feline body
wingless shoulders with decorative spiral plumage
description: Recovered from the Throne Room of the Palace of Knossos, this Late Minoan wall painting portrays heraldic griffins resting amidst swaying papyrus reeds and undulating sacred landscapes. Remarkably wingless, the creatures combine tawny leonine bodies with white eagle heads, scrolling neck spirals, and plumed crests to guard the epiphany of the ruler or priestess seated upon the gypsum throne.

title: Mycenaean Carved Ivory Pyxis with Winged Griffins Attacking Stags
originLocation: Athenian Agora (Tomb on the Areopagus), Athens, Greece
medium: Cylindrical elephant ivory cosmetic box carved in relief
creator: Mycenaean ivory carver
repository: Museum of the Ancient Agora, Athens
anatomy: raptor head with curved predatory beak
sweeping layered eagle wings
muscular lion hindquarters and taloned paws
curling feline tail
description: Excavated from a wealthy Late Bronze Age chamber tomb on the northern slope of the Areopagus in Athens, this cylindrical ivory pyxis captures the violent dynamism of Mycenaean animal combat. Fierce winged griffins plunge from rocky crags to sink their beaks and leonine claws into fleeing stags, blending Minoan naturalism with mainland heroic vigor.

title: Terracotta Centaur of Lefkandi (Chiron)
medium: Wheel-made and hand-modeled painted terracotta figurine
creator: Euboean Protogeometric potter-sculptor
anatomy: bearded human head and upright torso
cylindrical equine barrel painted with geometric hatching
six-fingered right hand
deliberate gash on the left foreleg knee
description: Deliberately broken in antiquity so that its head and body were buried in two adjacent tombs at Toumba in Lefkandi, this hollow terracotta statuette is the earliest monumental three-dimensional centaur in Greek art. Both its six-fingered hand and a deliberate incision on the left foreknee identify the wise centaur Chiron, wounded by Herakles' poisoned arrow.

title: Eleusis Proto-Attic Amphora: Odysseus Blinding the Cyclops Polyphemus
medium: Monumental Proto-Attic funerary neck-amphora in outline and black-and-white slip
creator: Polyphemus Painter
anatomy: colossal seated giant towering to the frame border
gaping mouth roaring in pain
single frontal eye socket pierced by a sharpened stake
drunken hand clutching a skyphos wine-cup
description: Standing 142 centimeters tall and used for a child's burial at Eleusis, the name-vase of the Polyphemus Painter bears on its neck one of the earliest narrative scenes from Homeric epic. Painted in white slip to distinguish the hero, Odysseus and two companions drive a long spit into the eye of the seated giant Polyphemus, who clutches the wine cup that lulled him into stupor.

title: Cast Bronze Griffin Cauldron Protome from Samos
originLocation: Heraion of Samos (attributed), Aegean Islands, Greece
medium: Hollow-cast bronze cauldron attachment with incised scales
creator: Samian Orientalizing bronze workshop
anatomy: gaping curved eagle beak with darting tongue
tall upright equine-like ears
central knobbed forehead forelock
sinuous scaly serpentine neck
description: Riveted in outward-facing rows around the rims of monumental bronze votive cauldrons dedicated at sanctuaries like the Samian Heraion—celebrated by Herodotus—this Orientalizing griffin protome transforms Near Eastern metalwork models into taut Greek sculptural form. Its wide-open raptor beak, upright ears, and tall forehead knob project fierce apotropaic vigilance.

title: West Pediment of the Temple of Artemis at Corfu: Archaic Gorgon Medusa
creator: Corinthian-Corcyraean sculptural workshop
anatomy: broad grimacing face with boar-like tusks and protruding tongue
writhing vipers coiled through braided locks
intertwined two-serpent girdle knotted at the waist
curved wings and archaic knielauf (kneeling-run) stance
description: Carved in local limestone as the centerpiece of Greece's oldest surviving monumental stone temple pediment, the terrifying Gorgon Medusa rushes forward in the archaic 'kneeling-run' posture. Framed by two recumbent panthers and her newly born offspring Pegasus and Chrysaor, her fanged grimace, protruding tongue, and belt of knotted serpents warded off malevolent forces from the sanctuary of Artemis.

title: Triple-Bodied Monster ('Bluebeard') from the Hekatompedon Pediment
creator: Attic Archaic Acropolis workshop
anatomy: three smiling bearded male torsos conjoined at the waist
dark blue-painted beards and hair
outspread polychrome wings
intertwined striped serpentine tails
description: Preserving vivid archaic pigments of dark blue, red, and green after being buried on the Acropolis following the Persian sack of 480 BCE, this poros limestone pedimental relief depicts a genial yet monstrous triple-bodied deity ending in twisting snake coils. Holding emblems of water, fire, and air (a bird) in his three left hands, the winged hybrid has been identified variously as Typhon, Proteus, Nereus, or the elemental Tritopatores.

title: Colossal Marble Sphinx of the Naxians at Delphi
originLocation: Sanctuary of Apollo, Delphi, Phocis, Greece
medium: Carved Naxian marble sculpture in the round
creator: Naxian Cycladic sculptor
anatomy: serene female face with archaic smile and braided kore locks
sickle-shaped upturned feathered wings
feathered breastplate over a taut seated feline body
powerful lion paws resting on an Ionic capital
description: Dedicated by the islanders of Naxos beside the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, this 2.22-meter marble sphinx originally crowned a towering ten-meter Ionic column overlooking the Pythian sanctuary. Blending the enigmatic archaic smile of a Cycladic kore with taut leonine haunches and sweeping sickle-curved wings, she served as a formidable chthonic guardian of the Delphic oracle.

title: Late Corinthian Black-Figure Amphora: Perseus, Andromeda, and Ketos
originLocation: Made in Corinth; excavated at Cerveteri (Caere), Italy
medium: Wheel-thrown ceramic neck-amphora in black-figure with added red and white
creator: Late Corinthian black-figure vase painter
anatomy: cavernous white-toothed jaws emerging from the sea
dog-like snout and glaring predatory eye
spiny dorsal crest
massive undulating marine trunk
description: Inscribed in archaic Corinthian script naming Perseus, Andromeda, and Ketos (ΚΕΤΟΣ), this black-figure amphora preserves the earliest known visual survival of the Andromeda myth. Rather than wielding Medusa's severed head, Perseus pelts the colossal fanged sea-monster's gaping white-toothed maw with boulders while Andromeda assists behind him.

title: Laconian Black-Figure Kylix: Odysseus and Companions Blinding Polyphemus
creator: Rider Painter
repository: Cabinet des Médailles, Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris (Inv. 190)
anatomy: hulking bearded cannibal giant seated on a rock
single brow eye impaled by a timber beam
severed human lower legs clutched in both hands
serpentine decorative exergue fish below
description: Compressing three moments of Odyssey Book 9 into a single circular tondo, the Laconian Rider Painter shows the monstrous Cyclops Polyphemus simultaneously devouring human limbs, accepting a kantharos of unmixed wine from Odysseus, and being blinded by four heroes hoisting a long stake. A large tuna swims in the exergue beneath their feet, anchoring the cave encounter to Odysseus' perilous sea voyage.

title: Chalcidian Black-Figure Hydria: Zeus Hurling His Thunderbolt at Winged Typhon
originLocation: Euboean-Chalcidian workshop (Rhegion); found at Vulci, Italy
creator: Inscription Painter
anatomy: bearded anthropoid upper torso and fierce glaring face
four expansive multicolored wings
twin coiling serpent legs replacing human limbs
forked scaly draconic tails
description: On the shoulder-and-belly frieze of this celebrated Chalcidian hydria, the storm-monster Typhon confronts Zeus's raised thunderbolt in a cosmic struggle for sovereignty over the heavens. Rendered with incised precision and rich purple-red highlights, Typhon combines a muscular bearded male torso and sweeping wings with twin writhing, scaly serpent coils in place of legs.

title: Attic Black-Figure Amphora: Theseus Slaying the Bull-Headed Minotaur
creator: Group of London B 174
anatomy: horned bovine bull head and thick muscled neck
athletic human male torso, arms, and legs
bovine tail hanging behind
hand brandishing a jagged boulder in defense
description: Flanked by Athenian youths and maidens sent as tribute to Crete, the youthful hero Theseus seizes the Minotaur by the horn and drives his sword deep into the monster's throat on this Attic black-figure amphora. Forced onto one knee while clutching a stone in vain resistance, the Cretan hybrid displays the canonical Greek iconography of a powerful human physique surmounted by a horned bull's head.

title: Caeretan Black-Figure Hydria: Herakles Presenting Cerberus to Terrified Eurystheus
originLocation: Ionian Greek immigrant workshop at Caere (Cerveteri)
medium: Polychrome black-figure terracotta hydria with red, white, and ochre slips
creator: Eagle Painter
anatomy: three snarling canine heads painted in black, red, and white
mane of venomous snakes sprouting along necks, paws, and back
coiling serpent-headed tail
massive hound body restrained on a leash
description: Painted with irrepressible comic flair by an East Greek master from Phocaea working in Caere, this hydria depicts Herakles hauling the Hound of Hades into the daylight while King Eurystheus dives headlong into a sunken storage pithos in terror. Cerberus bristles with coloristic ferocity: his three distinct dog heads—black, russet, and white—are ringed with a living mane of hissing vipers.

title: Caeretan Black-Figure Hydria: Herakles and Iolaos Battling the Lernaean Hydra
originLocation: Ionian Greek immigrant workshop at Caere (Cerveteri)
creator: Eagle Painter
repository: J. Paul Getty Museum, Getty Villa, Malibu (83.AE.346)
anatomy: nine long undulating serpentine necks
fanged dragon heads with forked darting tongues
thick braided central serpent trunk
coiled tail accompanied by Hera's pinching crab
description: Across the front of this vibrant Caeretan hydria, the nine-headed Lernaean Hydra rears up as a writhing knot of fanged serpents while Herakles clubs its necks and his nephew Iolaos cauterizes the stumps with a blazing sickle-brand. Beneath the monster's coils, a giant crab sent by Hera pinches Herakles' heel, capturing every detail of the hero's second labor.

title: Attic Black-Figure Kylix Tondo: Apotropaic Gorgoneion
medium: Attic black-figure ceramic kylix with added purple-red and white
creator: Leagros Group
repository: Cabinet des Médailles, Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris (Inv. 322)
anatomy: strictly frontal mask-like visage
wide staring eyes and furrowed brow
gaping grin baring four curved boar tusks
hanging blood-red tongue and fringed beard
description: Positioned at the center of an Attic black-figure drinking cup, this disembodied Gorgon mask (Gorgoneion) remained hidden beneath dark wine until a symposiast drained the vessel, suddenly locking eyes with Medusa's petrifying stare. Incised curls, glaring white sclera, four projecting tusks, and a bright crimson tongue exemplify the playfully terrifying theatricality of Archaic Greek banquet ware.

title: Attic Black-Figure Amphora: Herakles Wrestling the Sea-God Triton
creator: Pasikles Painter
repository: Museo Archeologico Regionale Paolo Orsi, Syracuse
anatomy: bearded wreathed male upper torso and arms
long scaly serpentine piscine body
serrated dorsal fin crest
forked fish caudal fin
description: Under the watchful gaze of Athena, Herakles locks his arms around the chest of the merman deity Triton, wrestling the elusive 'Old Man of the Sea' to extract directions to the Garden of the Hesperides. Triton's bearded human upper body transitions seamlessly at the waist into a long, intricately incised fish-scaled tail that coils across the amphora's panel.

title: Harpy Tomb Relief from Xanthos: Winged Female Creature Carrying a Soul
originLocation: Acropolis of Xanthos, Lycia (carved in East Greek Archaic style)
medium: Carved white marble tomb-chamber relief slab
creator: East Greek / Ionian sculptor at Xanthos
anatomy: archaic female head, coiffure, and human arms
plump ovoid bird body and feathered tail
broad layered eagle wings
raptor legs and talons clutching a diminutive human figure
description: Carved by East Greek sculptors for a dynastic pillar tomb at Xanthos, four winged bird-women soar away from enthroned rulers while tenderly cradling tiny human figures against their feathered breasts. Long known as 'Harpies' after Homer's snatching storm-spirits—though modern scholars also link them to benevolent Siren psychopomps—they embody the gentle transport of mortal souls to the afterlife.

title: Attic Red-Figure Kylix by Douris: The Colchian Dragon Regurgitating Jason
creator: Douris
anatomy: immense speckled serpent body with ventral belly plates
crested draconic head and fleshy chin beard
rows of sharp recurved teeth
distended jaws disgorging a full-grown hero
description: Preserving an otherwise lost variant of the Argonautic myth unknown to extant literary texts, the master vase-painter Douris depicts the sleepless Colchian Dragon regurgitating a limp, bearded Jason at the command of Athena, who stands calmly holding her owl and spear. Behind the giant bearded serpent, the Golden Fleece hangs gleaming from the branches of the sacred grove.

title: The Siren Vase: Attic Red-Figure Stamnos of Odysseus and the Sirens
originLocation: Athens, Attica, Greece (excavated at Vulci, Italy)
creator: Siren Painter (name-vase)
anatomy: diademed female human head with parted lips in song
plump speckled songbird body and fan tail
outspread feathered raptor wings
bird legs with sharp talons perched on sea-cliffs
description: The definitive ancient visualization of Homer's Sirens, this Early Classical stamnos shows Odysseus lashed tightly to the mast of his oared galley as his wax-deafened crew rows past rocky headlands. Two Sirens perch on opposing cliffs singing their fatal melody—one inscribed 'Himeropa' ('Voice of Yearning')—while a third plunges headfirst with closed eyes into the sea in suicide upon failing to lure the hero.

title: Attic Red-Figure Kylix: Oedipus Pondering the Riddle of the Theban Sphinx
originLocation: Athens, Attica, Greece (excavated at Vulci, Italy)
creator: Oedipus Painter
anatomy: diademed female head leaning forward in interrogation
seated leonine body perched atop an Ionic column
spotted and layered avian wings
tufted feline tail
description: Replacing physical combat with psychological tension, the tondo of this Attic red-figure kylix seats the winged Theban Sphinx high atop an Ionic column face-to-face with the weary traveler Oedipus, who rests chin-in-hand wearing his petasos hat and chlamys cloak. Painted inscriptions record a fragment of her deadly riddle ('and having three [feet]...'), immortalizing the triumph of human intellect over monstrous terror.

title: Melian Terracotta Relief Plaque of the Sea-Monster Scylla
originLocation: Made on Melos; excavated on Aegina, Greece
creator: Melian coroplastic workshop
anatomy: classical maiden head and upper torso
pack of snarling hounds springing from the groin and flanks
spiny coiled sea-serpent tail
finned marine crest
description: Produced on the Cycladic island of Melos as an ornamental chest or funerary attachment, this open-work terracotta plaque establishes the Classical visual form of Scylla, terror of the Strait of Messina. Unlike Homer's six-necked cave beast, Classical artists envisioned her as a graceful maiden from the waist up whose loins erupt into baying hunting dogs above a long, undulating ketos-like sea tail.

title: Attic Red-Figure Kylix Tondo: Equine-Tailed Silenus (Satyr) and Maenad
creator: Penthesilea Painter workshop
anatomy: bald forehead, snub nose, and shaggy beard
pointed equine ears
muscular human body
long bushy horse tail
description: Framed within a meander border on the interior of an Attic wine cup, a wild woodland satyr (silenos) confronts a thyrsus-bearing maenad from the ecstatic retinue of Dionysus. True to fifth-century Athenian convention—before Hellenistic syncretism with goat-legged Pan—the satyr possesses pointed equine ears, a snub-nosed bestial visage, and a flowing horse's tail.

title: Parthenon South Metope XXX: Centaur Triumphing Over a Fallen Lapith
creator: Workshop of Phidias
anatomy: furrowed bestial bearded face and muscular human chest
seamless anatomical transition at the ribcage and equine withers
rearing stallion barrel and hindquarters
sharp equine hooves trampling the adversary
description: Carved in Pentelic marble for the southern Doric frieze of the Parthenon under the supervision of Phidias, South Metope XXX dramatizes the mythical Centauromachy at the wedding of Peirithoos as an allegory of Greek order (nomos) threatened by untamed savagery (hybris). Rearing upon powerful equine hind legs while a panther skin swirls behind him, the centaur plunges his forehooves into the flank of a kneeling Lapith youth.

title: The Medusa Rondanini
civilization: Classical Greece (Roman Imperial copy after a 5th-century BCE Attic original)
originLocation: After an Athenian original of c. 440 BCE attributed to Phidias
dateDisplay: Original c. 440 BCE (marble copy 1st–2nd century CE)
creator: After Phidias (attributed)
anatomy: idealized sorrowful Classical female features
pair of small wings sprouting above the temples
undulating locks mingling with two scaled serpents
knotted snake tails tied beneath the chin
description: Widely regarded as a faithful marble reflection of the gilded Gorgoneion set by Phidias at the center of Athena Parthenos' shield, the Medusa Rondanini marks the pivotal transformation of the Gorgon from hideous archaic monster into a hauntingly beautiful woman. Two small wings rise from her brow while twin vipers frame her cheeks and knot their tails beneath her chin, freezing her visage in cool, tragic stillness.

title: Silver Didrachm of Knossos: Running Bull-Headed Minotaur
creator: Civic mint of Knossos
repository: Cabinet des Médailles, Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris
anatomy: horned bull head turned in profile
muscular nude human torso and striding legs
tufted bovine tail curving behind
hands clutching spherical throwing stones
description: Struck by the Classical Greek polis of Knossos—paired on its reverse with a geometric labyrinth emblem—this silver didrachm proudly adopts the city's legendary Bronze Age monster as its civic badge. Retaining the dynamic archaic kneeling-run pose within the circular coin flan, the bull-headed Minotaur brandishes stones in both hands as guardian of the Cretan labyrinth.

title: Corinthian Silver Stater ('Polos'): Winged Pegasus in Flight
creator: Civic mint of Corinth
anatomy: thoroughbred stallion head, neck, and hooves
sweeping feathered raptor wing with layered covert plumes
airborne galloping forelegs
archaic koppa (Ϙ) mintmark beneath the belly
description: So ubiquitous across Mediterranean trade that Corinthian silver staters were nicknamed pōloi ('colts'), this coin celebrates Pegasus, the immortal winged stallion tamed by Bellerophon at Corinth's sacred Peirene spring with Athena's golden bridle. Above the archaic letter koppa denoting Corinth, Pegasus surges skyward on finely engraved feathered pinions.

title: Funerary Marble Statue of a Mourning Siren Playing the Lyre
medium: Carved Pentelic marble funerary sculpture in the round
creator: Attic Classical sculptor
anatomy: youthful female head, breasts, and human torso
raised feathered wings framing the shoulders
feathered bird thighs transitioning at the hips
raptor legs and talons gripping a rocky plinth
description: Excavated in the Kerameikos necropolis of Athens, where it stood as an acroterial guardian beside grave monuments, this Pentelic marble Siren reimagines Homer's lethal temptress as a compassionate mourner for the dead. Blending a sensitively modeled female upper body with bird thighs, talons, and raised wings, she cradles a tortoiseshell lyre once strung with bronze wires to intone an eternal dirge.

title: Hellenistic Pebble Mosaic: Bellerophon on Pegasus Slaying the Chimera
medium: Polychrome natural river-pebble floor mosaic with lead strips
creator: Rhodian Hellenistic mosaicist
anatomy: tawny maned lion foreparts and roaring jaws
horned fire-breathing goat head sprouting from the spine
hissing serpent head forming the tail tip
paired confrontation with winged Pegasus overhead
description: Laid in finely graded natural pebbles of white, ochre, russet, and black for an elite dining room (andron) in ancient Rhodes, this early Hellenistic floor mosaic captures Bellerophon swooping down astride winged Pegasus to thrust his spear into the Lycian Chimera. True to Hesiod's formula—'lion in front, snake behind, and goat in the middle'—the tripartite beast snarls upward as a goat head erupts from its back and a viper lashes at its tail.

title: The Barberini Faun (Sleeping Satyr)
originLocation: Pergamene Hellenistic school (excavated near Castel Sant'Angelo, Rome)
creator: Pergamene Hellenistic sculptor
anatomy: ivy-wreathed tousled locks and snub-nosed rustic face
small pointed caprine-equine ears and neck glands (phereti)
hyper-muscular sprawling human physique
animal tail tucked onto the panther-skin rock
description: A tour de force of Hellenistic Baroque naturalism attributed to a Pergamene master, the over-life-size Barberini Faun portrays a drunken woodland satyr sprawled in restless, wine-heavy slumber across a panther pelt. Subtle bestial markers—pointed ears, arched brows, flared nostrils, and a tail resting against the rock—remind the viewer that this sensuous figure belongs to Dionysus's untamed wilderness.
